text_blocks.snippet: While there isn't a cure for Alzheimer's disease, several treatments can help manage symptoms and potentially slow disease progression, particularly in the early stages. These treatments include medications like cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine, as well as newer immunotherapies targeting amyloid proteins. Non-drug interventions like exercise, social engagement, and a calm environment also play a crucial role in managing the disease.
snippet_highlighted_words: medications like cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine, as well as newer immunotherapies targeting amyloid proteins

list.title: Cholinesterase Inhibitors:
list.snippet: These medications, such as donepezil (Aricept), rivastigmine (Exelon), and galantamine (Razadyne), are often prescribed for mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease. They work by increasing the levels of acetylcholine, a neurotransmitter involved in memory and thinking, which can help improve cognitive function.

list.title: Memantine:
list.snippet: This medication is typically used for moderate to severe Alzheimer's disease. It regulates glutamate, another brain chemical, which can be overproduced in Alzheimer's and potentially damage brain cells.

list.title: Immunotherapy:
list.snippet: Recent advancements include medications like lecanemab (Leqembi) and donanemab, which are approved for early-stage Alzheimer's (mild cognitive impairment and mild dementia). These monoclonal antibodies target and break down amyloid plaques in the brain, potentially slowing disease progression.
